metadata.title: Fixes that Fail - Generic Archetype
metadata.description: A generic representation of the Fixes that Fail archetype, where short-term solutions create unintended consequences that worsen the original problem over time. This creates two overlapping feedback loops: a balancing loop that provides temporary relief and a reinforcing loop that creates escalating problems.
learning_objectives: Understand the structure of the Fixes that Fail archetype
Recognize how short-term fixes can create long-term problems
Identify the difference between balancing and reinforcing loops
Explore how unintended consequences emerge from quick fixes
Learn to look for root causes rather than symptoms
metadata.author: Dan McCreary using Claude Sonnet 4.0
metadata.layout_strategy: The diagram uses a triangular layout with Problem on the left (300, 200), Fix on the right (700, 200), and Consequences at the bottom (500, 400). This creates clear visual separation between the two loops while showing their interconnection. The balancing loop (Short Term Fix) runs along the top between Problem and Fix, while the reinforcing loop (Unintended Consequences) includes all three nodes in a triangular pattern. Loop symbols are positioned to be clearly visible: the balancing loop symbol at (500, 150) and the reinforcing loop symbol at (500, 300).
metadata.notes: This is a generic template for the Fixes that Fail archetype. It can be adapted for specific situations by changing node labels and descriptions while maintaining the same fundamental structure. The key insight is that the balancing loop dominates initially (providing quick relief) but the reinforcing loop becomes dominant over time as consequences accumulate.

nodes.label: Problem
nodes.description: The original issue or challenge that triggers the need for action. This could be any type of problem requiring intervention.
nodes.measurement: Severity level, frequency of occurrence, impact assessment

nodes.label: Quick Fix
nodes.description: The immediate solution or intervention applied to address the problem. Often chosen for speed and apparent effectiveness rather than long-term sustainability.
nodes.measurement: Implementation speed, resource investment, scope of intervention

nodes.label: Unintended Consequences
nodes.description: The unforeseen negative side effects that emerge from the quick fix. These consequences often undermine the system's ability to solve the original problem.
nodes.measurement: Severity of side effects, time to emergence, scope of impact

edges.label: triggers
edges.description: The presence and severity of the problem drives the implementation of quick fixes

edges.label: temporarily reduces
edges.description: The quick fix provides immediate relief by reducing the problem symptoms

delay.description: Quick fixes typically show immediate results, which is why they're attractive

edges.label: creates
edges.description: The quick fix generates unintended consequences that weren't considered in the original solution

delay.description: Unintended consequences often take time to become apparent, making the connection to the fix difficult to see

edges.label: worsens
edges.description: The unintended consequences make the original problem worse or create conditions that prevent sustainable solutions

delay.description: The impact of consequences on the original problem often emerges slowly, creating significant delays in recognizing the pattern

loops.label: Short Term Fix Loop
loops.description: The quick fix.  The balancing loop where problems trigger quick fixes that temporarily reduce the problem symptoms
loops.behavior_pattern: Provides immediate relief and temporary stability
loops.dominance_conditions: Dominant in the short term when quick fixes show immediate results

loops.label: Unintended Consequences Loop
loops.description: The unintended consequences. The reinforcing loop where fixes create consequences that worsen the original problem, leading to more fixes and worse consequences
loops.behavior_pattern: Creates escalating problems and increasing dependence on quick fixes
loops.dominance_conditions: Becomes dominant over time as consequences accumulate and compound

leverage_points.title: Address Root Causes Instead of Symptoms
leverage_points.description: Focus on understanding and addressing the fundamental causes of problems rather than just treating symptoms
intervention_strategies: Invest time in thorough problem analysis before implementing solutions
Use root cause analysis techniques like 5 Whys or fishbone diagrams
Engage diverse stakeholders to understand different perspectives on the problem
leverage_points.expected_impact: Prevents the cycle from starting by solving problems at their source
examples: Improving training programs instead of just fixing individual mistakes
Redesigning processes instead of adding more oversight

leverage_points.title: Anticipate and Plan for Unintended Consequences
leverage_points.description: Before implementing fixes, systematically consider what negative side effects might occur
intervention_strategies: Use pre-mortem analysis to imagine how solutions might fail
Pilot test solutions on a small scale before full implementation
Create monitoring systems to detect early signs of unintended consequences
leverage_points.expected_impact: Reduces the severity of unintended consequences by preparing for them
examples: Testing new policies in one department before organization-wide rollout
Including sunset clauses in temporary measures

leverage_points.title: Create Systems to Detect Long-term Impacts
leverage_points.description: Establish monitoring and feedback systems that can detect the delayed effects of interventions
intervention_strategies: Set up long-term tracking metrics beyond immediate results
Create regular review cycles to assess intervention effectiveness
Establish early warning indicators for system degradation
leverage_points.expected_impact: Enables earlier detection of when fixes are creating problems
examples: Tracking employee satisfaction after productivity interventions
Monitoring system reliability after quick performance fixes

scenarios.title: Continue Using Quick Fixes
scenarios.description: The system continues to rely on quick fixes whenever problems arise, without addressing underlying causes

changes.change_description: Quick fix response becomes automatic and faster

scenarios.predicted_outcomes: Escalating problems as consequences accumulate, increasing system instability, and growing dependence on fixes that create more problems than they solve

scenarios.title: Shift to Root Cause Solutions
scenarios.description: The system changes approach to focus on identifying and addressing fundamental causes rather than symptoms

changes.change_description: Solutions target root causes instead of symptoms

scenarios.predicted_outcomes: Slower initial progress but sustainable improvements, reduced unintended consequences, and increased system resilience over time

scenarios.title: Balance Quick Fixes with Long-term Solutions
scenarios.description: The system uses quick fixes for immediate relief while simultaneously working on root cause solutions

changes.change_description: Consequences are anticipated and mitigated through parallel long-term solutions

scenarios.predicted_outcomes: Managed short-term stability while building long-term capabilities, reduced severity of unintended consequences

discussion_questions: Why do quick fixes often seem more attractive than long-term solutions?
How do delays in feedback make it difficult to see the connection between fixes and consequences?
What role does organizational pressure play in promoting quick fixes over root cause solutions?
How can you distinguish between treating symptoms and addressing root causes?
What are some strategies for managing the tension between immediate relief and long-term solutions?
key_insights: Quick fixes create a balancing loop that provides temporary relief but may trigger a reinforcing loop of escalating problems
Unintended consequences often emerge with significant delays, making their connection to the original fix difficult to see
The short-term effectiveness of fixes can mask their long-term negative impacts
Systems thinking requires considering both immediate and delayed effects of interventions
Breaking the cycle requires shifting focus from symptoms to root causes

common_misconceptions.misconception: If a fix works immediately, it's a good solution
common_misconceptions.correction: Immediate effectiveness doesn't guarantee long-term success; unintended consequences may emerge later

common_misconceptions.misconception: Quick fixes are always bad and should never be used
common_misconceptions.correction: Quick fixes can be appropriate for immediate relief if paired with long-term root cause solutions

common_misconceptions.misconception: Unintended consequences are unpredictable and unavoidable
common_misconceptions.correction: Many unintended consequences can be anticipated through systems thinking and careful analysis

extension_activities: Identify a 'Fixes that Fail' pattern in your personal or professional life
Practice root cause analysis using techniques like the 5 Whys method
Design a monitoring system to detect unintended consequences of a recent change
Compare the short-term and long-term costs of quick fixes versus root cause solutions
